transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well… I guess what finally got me to come in is that I’m tired of working my whole life around avoiding things. I’ve got a workshop at home—used to spend a lot of time out there, you know, puttering around, fixing things, keeping my hands busy—but I keep steering clear of it now. And it’s not just that. Family get-togethers have become something I plan around too, especially if there’s any chance my brother-in-law might be there.

I know that probably sounds like a small thing, or maybe just family awkwardness, but after all this time it feels like I’m arranging my days so I don’t run into reminders. I’ll make excuses, stay home, find reasons not to go near certain places or people. And I’m 76 years old—I don’t really want to keep living like I’m dodging parts of my own life. So… that’s what brings me in, I suppose.
Do you find yourself feeling anxious or fearful in social situations, especially when you expect scrutiny or judgment from others?

I’m not sure I’d put it that way, no. I mean, I don’t love being the center of attention—never really have—but I can’t say I’m sitting there worried everyone’s judging me or watching for me to mess up.

If I get uneasy around people, it’s usually more about who might be there or what the situation reminds me of, not so much feeling scrutinized. Like at a big family thing, I might be tense, but it isn’t because I think they’re all looking down on me. It’s… well, it’s hard to explain, but “fear of judgment” doesn’t quite sound like what I experience.
When you avoid certain people or places, like your workshop or family gatherings, does it bring up memories or feelings connected to a specific time when something upsetting happened to you?

Yes… yes, that’s pretty much it. It’s not just that I don’t feel like going into the workshop, or that I’d rather skip a family gathering because I’m tired or something. It’s more like those places—or certain people being there—set off this whole chain of memories and feelings I’d rather not get into.

The workshop especially… I used to like being out there. It was my space, you know? But now I’ll find myself walking toward it and then turning around, making some excuse like I need to do something in the house first. And with family things, if I hear my brother-in-law might be there, I start figuring out ways not to go before I’ve even thought it through.

So yes, I guess I came in because I’m tired of steering clear of my own workshop and any get-together where he might be, and after all this time I’m worn out from planning my life around not running into those reminders.

Can you tell me more about those memories or feelings that come up when you think about your workshop or being around your brother-in-law? Do they feel like sudden, vivid recollections of something specific that happened?

Yes… they do. Not like I’m sitting down and deciding to remember it, more like it just… arrives. Out of nowhere.

It can be the strangest times, too. I’ll be shaving in the morning, just looking in the mirror, not thinking about anything in particular, and suddenly I’ll see his hand again. His hand holding that heavy tool. It’s like a picture popping into my head, very clear for a second, and I get this tightness in my chest before I’ve even had time to tell myself, “That’s not happening now.”

Same thing can happen when I’m working on a painting. I’ll be focused on a brushstroke or a color, and then there it is again, that image. Not the whole thing always, just that piece of it—his hand, the weight of the tool, the feeling that comes with it. And I don’t mean I’m trying to dwell on it. I’d rather not think about it at all. But it comes up anyway, and even now, after all this time, my body reacts like it matters right this minute.
When these memories come up, do you find yourself feeling the same fear, anger, or other strong emotions you felt during that original event?

Yes… I do. Maybe not every single time in the exact same way, but when that picture comes into my head, it’s like my body reacts before I can get a handle on it.

I’ll just be shaving, or working on a painting, and out of nowhere I see his hand again with that heavy tool. Just that piece of it, like a snapshot that pops up without me asking for it. And my chest tightens right away. It’s not just “remembering” in the normal sense, like thinking back on something old. It brings that feeling with it, that rush… fear, mostly, and something else too, like being braced for what’s coming.

I try to tell myself, “You’re standing here now, you’re just holding a razor,” or “You’re just painting,” but for a moment it doesn’t feel that simple. It feels too close. Even after all this time, it can still hit me hard.
Do you find yourself often feeling on edge, angry, or tense, even when you’re not thinking about those memories?

Yes… I think so. It’s not only when the memories are right there in front of me. Even when I’m doing something ordinary, I feel like part of me is sort of… scanning.

Like at the senior center, for example, or in the church basement after service, places where I should feel perfectly fine. I’ll still catch myself checking who came in, where the door is, who’s moving around. If someone stands too close behind me, I notice it right away. I don’t mean to make a big show of it, but I’ll shift my chair or turn myself a little so I can see better.

It’s tiring, honestly, because I know most of the time nothing is happening. These are people having coffee, talking about the weather, normal things. But I’m still watching the room like I need to be ready for something. It’s like I can’t quite relax unless I know where everyone is.
Do you often have trouble sleeping, or do you wake up in the middle of the night because of disturbing thoughts or memories?

Yes… sleep is a little difficult for me. Most nights I can get myself to bed, and I’ll be tired enough, but then once the house is quiet I start listening. Every little sound seems bigger at night — a creak, the furnace, something outside — and I’ll lie there trying to decide if it’s nothing or if I should get up and check.

And then sometimes I do fall asleep, but I’ll wake up from a bad dream about the workshop. It’s not always the whole thing laid out like a movie, but enough of it that I wake up with that feeling in me. Then I’m just wide awake. I’ll look at the clock, and it might only be two or three in the morning, and I know I should just roll over and go back to sleep, but I can’t. My mind is already going, and my body feels like it’s still reacting.

It can take an hour, sometimes two, before I settle down again. I don’t know if I’d say it’s every single night, but it’s often enough that I notice it. It makes the nights feel long.
Have you found yourself believing things like 'I can't trust anyone,' 'the world is dangerous,' or 'I'm a bad person' since this started happening?

Yes… I suppose I have, though I don’t like admitting that. It sounds too hard, maybe too unfair, when I say it plainly.

I used to think family was the one place where you didn’t have to keep your guard up. You know, whatever else was going on in the world, at least the people who sat at your own table were safe. That was just how I was raised to think about it. Family might argue, sure, people get cross or say foolish things, but underneath it there was supposed to be trust.

Now I catch myself thinking… well, maybe you can’t really trust anyone. Not completely. Even people close to you. Even people you think you know. And I don’t want to be that kind of man, suspicious and bitter, looking at everybody sideways. But the thought comes in anyway. It’s like something in me learned the wrong lesson, or maybe learned a lesson I wish wasn’t true.

I don’t go around saying it out loud, and I try not to treat everyone like they’ve done something wrong. But inside, yes, there’s this belief now that people can turn on you, even the ones who are supposed to be closest. That’s been hard to shake.
Do you often feel angry, guilty, or ashamed about what happened during that event, or find yourself blaming yourself for it?

Yes… guilt, mostly. And shame too, I suppose, though I don’t like that word much.

I keep going back over it in my head, asking myself why I didn’t put my foot down sooner. I should have said no. I should have been firmer from the start and never let him stay with us. I tell myself, “You’re the man of the house, you should’ve handled it.” And then I start thinking maybe none of this would have happened if I’d acted differently, if I’d handled it like a man instead of trying to keep the peace.

I know people might say I couldn’t have known, or that I’m being too hard on myself, but that doesn’t stop the thought from coming. It sits there. Like I failed in some basic way I should’ve understood at my age.
Do you find yourself feeling angry, guilty, or ashamed specifically about what happened during that event, or do those feelings come and go depending on your mood?

It’s more tied to what happened, I’d say. I mean, my mood can make it louder or quieter, sure, but the thought itself is about that day, that whole situation.

I keep coming back to this idea that I should have put my foot down sooner. I should have said, “No, you’re not staying here,” and meant it. Instead I tried to be reasonable, tried to keep things calm, and now I look back and think maybe that was weakness. Like I didn’t do what I was supposed to do.

And I know that may sound old-fashioned, but I keep thinking, I was supposed to handle it like a man. I was supposed to protect my home, make the hard decision, not just hope things would work out. So yes, the guilt and shame come from that specifically — from believing maybe none of this would’ve happened if I’d been firmer right from the start.
How long have you been experiencing these memories, feelings of being on edge, and trouble sleeping?

It’s been… well, since that confrontation with my brother-in-law. That was about two years and four months ago now, give or take.

I don’t mean it was every single minute from that day forward, like a switch flipped and stayed exactly the same. But that’s when it started, and it’s been hanging around in one form or another ever since. I keep thinking maybe it should have eased up by now, after that much time, but when I count it out… yes, about two years and four months.

doctor.question: How long have you been experiencing these memories, feelings of being on edge, and trouble sleeping?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on since that confrontation with my brother-in-law about two years and four months ago.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking how long the PTSD-related symptoms have been occurring, which directly matches the duration item.

patient.answer:
It’s been… well, since that confrontation with my brother-in-law. That was about two years and four months ago now, give or take.

I don’t mean it was every single minute from that day forward, like a switch flipped and stayed exactly the same. But that’s when it started, and it’s been hanging around in one form or another ever since. I keep thinking maybe it should have eased up by now, after that much time, but when I count it out… yes, about two years and four months.

opening_question.intent: Identify the patient's primary concern or reason for seeking help
opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets criteria for PTSD (F43.11) based on exposure to a traumatic event involving actual or threatened serious harm, persistent re-experiencing of the event through intrusive memories and physiological reactions, persistent avoidance of reminders, negative alterations in cognition and mood (e.g., mistrust of others, self-blame), and marked alterations in arousal and reactivity (e.g., hypervigilance, sleep disturbance). Symptoms have persisted for over two months and cause clinically significant distress in daily functioning.
